title: “YOUR LOVE IS BETTER THAN WINE”: Why Does Scripture Compare Romantic Love to Intoxication?
paragraphs: “YOUR LOVE IS BETTER THAN WINE”: Why Does Scripture Compare Romantic Love to Intoxication?

Song of Songs 1:2 contains one of the Bible’s most startling descriptions of desire—and hidden inside it is a truth about love, longing, intimacy, and the human heart that many Christians were never taught how to talk about.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth…”
That is in your Bible.
Not hidden in an obscure manuscript.
Not whispered by some embarrassed lover outside the boundaries of Scripture.
Right there.
In holy Scripture.
Then comes the line that makes the verse even more startling:
כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Ki-tovim dodekha mi-yayin.
“For your love is better than wine.”
Song of Songs 1:2.
Read it again.
Slowly.
Because perhaps somewhere along the way, some of us learned a version of Christianity that knew how to talk about temptation but became strangely uncomfortable talking about desire.
We learned how to say, “Don’t.”
Don’t lust.
Don’t fornicate.
Don’t commit adultery.
Don’t cross the boundary.
And those warnings matter.
Jesus takes sexual holiness so seriously that He reaches beyond outward behavior into the desires of the heart.
But if all we ever hear is what sexuality can become when corrupted by sin, we can accidentally forget something Scripture never forgot:
God created love before humanity corrupted it.
Desire was not invented in a nightclub.
Romance was not invented by Hollywood.
The human body was not designed by pornography.
Marriage was not humanity’s attempt to domesticate lust.
Before there was adultery, there was covenant.
Before there was pornography, there was nakedness without shame.
Before lust twisted desire into consumption, God created man and woman and declared His creation “very good.”
And somewhere inside the canon of Scripture sits an entire book in which lovers notice each other.
Long for each other.
Praise each other.
Search for each other.
Delight in each other.
And speak with a startling emotional and physical intensity.
The Song of Songs refuses to pretend that holy love must be emotionally cold.
That matters.
Because there are people reading this who have spent years believing that holiness means becoming less human.
It does not.
Jesus did not come to make you less human.
He came to redeem what sin has disfigured.
And that brings us back to those ancient Hebrew words:
כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן

The word דֹּדֶיךָ — dodekha comes from dod, a word associated here with love, affection, or expressions of romantic love. The JPS rendering captures the thought as, “your love is more delightful than wine.”
Then comes מִיָּיִן — mi-yayin.
“Than wine.”
Why wine?
Why would inspired Scripture put romantic love beside something capable of producing exhilaration?
Because comparison is not necessarily endorsement of everything associated with the thing being compared.
Song of Songs 1:2 does not say, “Become drunk.”
It says, in effect:
Your love surpasses wine.

Wine belonged to the sensory world of the ancient biblical writers. It could signify celebration, abundance, festivity, pleasure, and gladness, while Scripture elsewhere also gives unmistakable warnings about drunkenness and loss of self-control.
So this is not a biblical excuse for intoxication.
It is poetry.
And poetry reaches for something you can feel in order to describe something difficult to measure.
Think about what happens when someone you deeply love walks into a room.
Suddenly you notice everything.
Their voice.
Their laugh.
The way they look at you.
The smallest touch becomes enormous.
A message from them can change your afternoon.
Their absence can make a crowded room feel empty.
Their presence can make an ordinary Tuesday feel like somebody secretly turned the lights brighter.
Love does something to perception.
That is part of the force of the image.
The woman in the Song is not clinically describing affection.
She is overwhelmed by it.
His love is not merely acceptable.
Not merely appropriate.
Not merely useful.
It is better than wine.

And maybe that bothers us because we have become comfortable with a Christianity that can discuss doctrine without trembling, marriage without romance, purity without beauty, and obedience without delight.
But the Bible is not embarrassed by delight.
Sin is not defeated by pretending pleasure does not exist.
Sin is defeated when pleasure is returned to its rightful place beneath the lordship of God.
That distinction changes everything.
Because lust says:
I want your body for me.
Love says:
I want your good, even when it costs me.
Lust consumes.
Love gives.
Lust separates pleasure from covenant and responsibility.
Love willingly binds pleasure to faithfulness.
Lust asks, “How much can I take?”
Covenant asks, “How faithfully can I give?”
And suddenly Song of Songs begins exposing something deeper than romance.
It exposes our counterfeit versions of love.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that means.
You thought obsession was love because it kept you awake at night.
You thought jealousy was love because somebody was terrified of losing control over you.
You thought sexual attention meant you were valuable.
You thought being wanted meant being cherished.
You thought chemistry meant covenant.
You thought because someone could make your heart race, they deserved access to your heart.
Maybe you gave pieces of yourself away because you were desperate to hear someone say:
“I choose you.”
Maybe somebody said it.
Then left.
Maybe the person who once made you feel intoxicated eventually became the person whose name you could barely say without feeling something break inside you.
And now this verse sounds different.
“Your love is better than wine.”
Because wine wears off.
Infatuation can wear off.
Adrenaline wears off.
Beauty changes.
Bodies age.
Feelings fluctuate.
The late-night conversations eventually meet morning responsibilities.

The wedding photographs eventually become mortgage payments, dirty dishes, sick children, misunderstandings, exhaustion, forgiveness, and the thousand ordinary decisions through which covenant either deepens or dies.
Biblical love was never supposed to survive merely because two people remained intoxicated with each other.
The feeling may begin the song.
Faithfulness must learn to carry it.
That is why the Song is so beautiful.
It celebrates desire without making desire God.
And Christianity does something even more radical.
It points beyond every human love toward the One for whom the human heart was ultimately made.
We should be careful here.

Song of Songs is genuinely love poetry. We do not need to erase the man and woman from the poem in order to make the book spiritual. Jewish and Christian interpreters have also historically seen theological dimensions in the Song, but its celebration of human love should not simply be dissolved into allegory.
Yet within the whole biblical story, even the greatest human love cannot carry the weight of being our Savior.
Your husband cannot be Jesus for you.
Your wife cannot be Jesus for you.
Your boyfriend cannot save you.
Your girlfriend cannot heal every wound inside you.
Marriage cannot bear the weight of worship.
Romance cannot forgive your sins.
Sex cannot reconcile you to God.
Another human being cannot become the answer to the deepest ache of your soul.
And many of our heartbreaks begin when we ask human love to accomplish what only divine grace can do.
We ask someone:
“Make me enough.”
“Make me secure.”
“Tell me I matter.”
“Never disappoint me.”
“Never leave me emotionally hungry.”
“Fill every empty room inside me.”
Then two sinners stand before each other carrying expectations that belong to God.
Eventually somebody collapses under the weight.
Maybe both do.
This is where the Gospel enters the love story.
Not to destroy romance.
To rescue it from becoming an idol.
Because Jesus does not merely teach you how to find love.
Jesus shows you what love ultimately looks like.
A cross.
Not sentimentality.
Not butterflies.
Not attraction without sacrifice.
A blood-stained cross outside Jerusalem where the Son of God gave Himself for sinners who could never repay Him.
Romans 5 does not say Christ died for us after we became attractive enough.
He loved us while we were sinners.
That is scandalous love.
We cheated on God with our idols.
We wanted His gifts without His presence.
We chased pleasure while ignoring the Giver.
We worshiped bodies, money, approval, attention, status, romance, ourselves.
We wanted creation without Creator.
And instead of abandoning rebels to the consequences of rebellion, God sent His Son.
Jesus lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And now forgiveness is offered not to people who successfully hide their scandal, but to people who bring their scandal into the light and trust the Savior.
That is why grace is so shocking.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace calls sinners home.
Maybe your romantic history is messy.
Maybe there are names you regret.
Beds you regret.
Messages you wish you had never sent.
Promises you broke.
Pictures you wish had never existed.
A marriage you damaged.
An affair nobody knows about.
A secret addiction behind an immaculate Christian profile.
Maybe you have learned how to lift your hands in worship while carrying shame you refuse to name.
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ is not waiting for a cleaner version of you before He invites you to repent.
Bring the real story.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the church version.
Not the version where you conveniently become the victim in every chapter.
Bring the chapter where you were wrong.
Bring the desire.
Bring the lust.
Bring the adultery.
Bring the pornography.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the loneliness.
Bring the relationship you know you have placed above God.
Bring the wounds other people inflicted upon you.
Bring the wounds you inflicted upon others.
Bring the thing you keep deleting from your browser but cannot delete from your conscience.
Bring it into His light.
Repentance is not Jesus humiliating you.
It is Jesus calling you out of the tomb you decorated because you were afraid to admit it was killing you.
And grace is not permission to return to chains.
Grace teaches us to belong to Christ.
Maybe that is what someone needs to hear tonight.
You do not need another counterfeit intoxication.
You need truth.
You need grace.
You need the Christ who knows exactly what happened and still calls sinners to Himself.
There is a reason counterfeit intimacy leaves people thirsty.
It promises transcendence but cannot sustain it.
It whispers, “One more person.”
“One more fantasy.”
“One more affair.”
“One more night.”
“One more message.”
“One more secret.”
“One more swipe.”
“One more body.”
And after “one more” comes another one.
Because lust is a terrible god.
It always wants another sacrifice.
Jesus is different.
At the cross, He became the sacrifice.
That is the Gospel.
And when Christ becomes Lord of our desires, He does not teach us to hate love.
He teaches us how to love without worshiping love.
He teaches husbands that love is sacrificial.
He teaches wives and husbands covenant faithfulness.
He teaches singles that their worth is not suspended until somebody chooses them.
He teaches the sexually broken that shame does not have to write the final chapter.
He teaches the lonely that loneliness is painful without making loneliness their identity.
He teaches the married that covenant is deeper than chemistry.
He teaches all of us that desire makes a terrible master but can become a beautiful servant when surrendered to God.
Then Song of Songs 1:2 can be heard without embarrassment.
“Let him kiss me…”
There is tenderness here.
Desire.
Delight.
And:
“Your love is better than wine.”
Not because losing control is holy.
But because faithful love can produce a delight that the poet reaches toward wine to describe—and then says love is better.
Better.
There is a word worth carrying home.
Some of us have settled for things that temporarily numb us because we have forgotten there are things worth loving that actually awaken us.
We settle for pornography instead of intimacy.
Attention instead of covenant.
Being desired instead of being known.
Fantasy instead of faithfulness.
Temporary intoxication instead of enduring love.
And sometimes we even settle for romantic love itself when Christ is standing at the center of history saying that no created person was ever designed to become our ultimate treasure.
Human love can be beautiful.
Marriage can be breathtaking.
A kiss can be holy within its proper covenantal home.
Desire can be received as part of God's created goodness.
But only Jesus can redeem the sinner.
Only Jesus can cleanse the conscience.
Only Jesus conquered death.
Only Jesus can take the scandal you thought would define you forever and write grace across the final page.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming sinners from it.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to explain the details publicly.
But perhaps you need to stop pretending.
There is no shame in admitting you need prayer.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not fighting alone.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be quietly drowning in a relationship they call love.
Somebody may think their sexual past has disqualified them from grace.
Somebody may be married and wondering where the tenderness went.
Somebody may be single and secretly wondering whether being unwanted romantically means being unwanted by God.
Somebody may love Jesus publicly while fighting sexual sin privately.
Put truth where they might find it.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what we knew clearly yesterday.
Come back when feelings become louder than truth.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow with you. Our desire is to keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ into places where hurting people can encounter it.

Scripture gives a real basis for materially supporting Gospel ministry. Paul writes that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from Gospel ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14). But Scripture also protects the heart of the giver: “not reluctantly or under compulsion”—God loves willing, cheerful generosity (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Those claims would go beyond what Scripture says.
Instead, if you prayerfully choose to support Gospel Warrior, let it be an offering freely given to help Gospel-centered teaching reach farther.
Give yourself to Christ.
Money cannot purchase grace.
An offering cannot erase sin.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Your deepest need is not membership in a ministry.
Your deepest need is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
So repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him your desires.
Bring Him your relationships.
Bring Him your sexuality.
Bring Him your marriage.
Bring Him your singleness.
Bring Him your loneliness.
Bring Him your shame.
Bring Him the love story that collapsed.
Bring Him the secret chapter.
Bring Him the person you still cannot forgive.
Bring Him the part of your heart that keeps reaching for another cup because the last one could not satisfy you.
Maybe you finally understand why that ancient line still burns after thousands of years:
כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Ki-tovim dodekha mi-yayin.
“Your love is better than wine.”
Human love can be intoxicating in the poetic sense—exhilarating, consuming, deeply delightful.
But even the sweetest human love is still a signpost.
It cannot become the destination of the soul.
Because eventually every earthly cup runs empty.
Every beautiful face grows older.
Every human heart reveals its limitations.
Every romance discovers that feelings alone cannot carry eternity.
And when every lesser cup finally reaches its bottom, Christ remains.
The Bridegroom who does not exploit.
The Savior who does not abandon repentant sinners.
The King who does not love you because you were spotless, but who gave Himself to cleanse and redeem His people.
The One whose grace reaches into bedrooms, broken marriages, secret addictions, lonely apartments, shattered engagements, guilty consciences, and stories we thought could never become testimonies.
So perhaps the question underneath Song of Songs 1:2 was never merely:
Why does Scripture compare romantic love to wine?
Perhaps it also forces us to ask:
What have I been drinking from because I am desperately thirsty to be loved?
And once that question reaches the heart, another follows.
What if the thing I keep asking another human being to give me can only finally be found in Jesus Christ?
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is reaching for another counterfeit cup.
Maybe your share will reach them first.
Maybe the resources you help sustain will put the words of Scripture in front of someone moments before they make a decision they cannot easily undo.
But ultimately, Gospel Warrior cannot save them.
You cannot save them.
I cannot save them.
Jesus can.
And perhaps that is the line worth remembering when everything else fades:
The world will keep offering you cups that make you forget your emptiness for a night; Jesus offers grace that can rewrite the story you thought you would carry forever.
